messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Anna Müller is a 54-year-old married woman who has worked for years as a chef, someone used to heat, pressure, and close quarters with other people moving quickly around her. When she first began describing the assault, it was striking how often she stopped and lost words. She could circle around parts of it, but she could not seem to tell it as a single story. What came instead were disconnected pieces: the scrape of a chair, a man stepping too close, the smell of stale alcohol, the shock of realizing that this was someone she had trusted and that she was not safe with him after all. She spoke of the event as if it lived more in her body than in language. At moments in session she would stiffen, her shoulders curling and her arms drawing inward, and say that when it came back to her she felt herself in the same position again, as though her body had gone back there before her mind could catch up. What frightened her most was not only that she had been assaulted, but that it had happened with someone she had believed she knew. She had come away certain that you can never know who will harm you, and that people cannot be trusted.

In the weeks afterward, Anna found that reminders appeared in places that had once felt ordinary. Certain kinds of conversation became unbearable, especially when talk turned personal or emotionally intimate, or when other people spoke in ways that edged toward trust, loyalty, or relationships. She would feel herself going tight and distant, as if she had to get out of the exchange before something dangerous happened. Emotional closeness itself began to feel risky. Even with people who cared about her, there was a sense that if she let them come too near, she would be exposed again. Being alone with men became especially difficult. She did not describe this as a vague discomfort; to her it felt like common sense. She was convinced that harm could come from anyone, and that the worst part was never seeing it clearly until it was too late.

These fears entered her workday in concrete ways. In the kitchen, where staff moved fast behind one another with knives, pans, and trays, unexpected movement nearby could make Anna jerk violently, her heart hammering as if she were in immediate danger. If a male coworker stepped beside her without warning or she found herself alone with a delivery driver in the back corridor, her whole body went on alert. She began positioning herself so she could see entrances and keep others in view. She watched strangers closely, even in ordinary situations, feeling threatened if one approached her on the street, in a store, or near the restaurant. She noticed where exits were, who was standing too near, whose footsteps were behind her. Hyperalertness had become part of how she moved through the day.

At home, this narrowing of safety affected her marriage. She was still living with her husband, but closeness had become complicated. It was not that she no longer cared for him; rather, emotional nearness itself could set off the same need to pull back. Conversations that might once have brought comfort now felt dangerous if they came too close to trust, hurt, or dependence. She kept parts of herself sealed off because she no longer believed that trusting someone protected you. The betrayal she felt in the assault remained central: she had trusted, and trust had not kept her safe. That conviction sat alongside her watchfulness, her fear around men, and her recoil from strangers.

By the time she sought help, Anna was exhausted by living as if danger were always one movement away. She was still working, but with increasing strain, and the kitchen had become a place where she was perpetually braced. She dreaded those moments when memory arrived not as a narrative she could recount, but as jagged pieces and bodily states she could not control or explain. Part of what finally brought her in was the recognition that she could no longer speak about what had happened without losing the thread entirely, and that more and more of her life was being organized around keeping distance from conversations, from men, and from closeness itself. She came to treatment wanting, above all, to feel less constantly endangered. At the same time, she was deeply afraid that if she let down her guard or trusted anyone enough to tell the story fully, she would once again discover too late that trust was exactly what put her at risk.
